Saturday, 4 May 2030, 3 p.m., in the wedding room of the town hall of Lyon’s 1st arrondissement. The registrar is a deputy mayor with glasses and a warm voice. Witnesses: Ioana and Chloé for Radu, Julien and a cousin from Salamanca for Lucia.
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. We are gathered here today to celebrate the marriage of Radu Popescu and Lucia García. Before we begin, I must check that the witnesses are present.
Present. Well… I think. I cried so much this morning that I’m not sure I’m still here.
(smiles) I will now read you the articles of the Civil Code. Spouses owe each other respect, fidelity, support and assistance. Together they ensure the moral and material direction of the family.
(very quietly, to Radu) Did you hear? Moral and material direction. That means I’m in charge of the budget.
(very quietly) It means “together”. But I’ll leave you the budget if you leave me the choice of music.
Lucia García, do you take Radu Popescu, here present, to be your husband?
Yes. Sí. Da. In every language I know.
Radu Popescu, do you take Lucia García, here present, to be your wife?
(steps back) Well… I think the whole arrondissement heard you. I declare you united in marriage. You may exchange rings.
(laughing) Why did you shout like that? You scared me!
Because someone asked me to say it loud enough to be heard up there. I’ll explain later.
Ladies and gentlemen, I present Mr and Mrs Popescu-García. You may applaud.

On Saturday 4 May, Radu woke at five in the morning, without an alarm. He lay in the dark with his eyes open, listening to the sounds of rue d’Austerlitz: a delivery van, a cat, the distant bells of Fourvière. He had Hélène’s envelope under his pillow. He hadn’t reread it. He knew it by heart.

At seven, the grandmother knocked on the door with a plate of cozonac and a bowl of hot milk. Radu said he wasn’t hungry. The grandmother didn’t answer. She sat on the edge of the bed, folded her arms, and waited. After five minutes, Radu had eaten three slices of cozonac. Some battles are lost in advance.

At the hotel, on the other side of the Saône, doña Carmen was dressing Lucia. The dress, which she had sewn in secret for three months, was white, simple, with Andalusian lace sleeves. Nobody had seen it, not even Pilar. When Lucia put it on, her mother started crying, and doña Carmen had to forbid her to come near, for fear she would wet the lace.

Then doña Carmen turned up the hem of the dress, and Lucia discovered a surprise. Inside the hem, sewn by hand, was a narrow strip of embroidered cloth, red and black, with patterns she didn’t know. “Radu’s grandmother sent it to me in March,” doña Carmen explained. “A piece of her own ie. So that you wear a little Romania all day.”

Lucia looked at her grandmother, astonished. So the two old ladies, who spoke no common language, had been plotting by post for months, without anyone knowing. “How did you do it?” Lucia asked. Doña Carmen shrugged. “With drawings. And with little Ioana, who translated without knowing what she was translating.”

At half past two, there was already a small crowd in front of the town hall of the 1st arrondissement. The two families, the colleagues from the office, Nathalie in a blue dress, Chloé in a red suit, Karim and Leïla, Odile on Isabelle’s arm, Mrs Roux in her wheelchair. And, a little apart, the sixty children of the orchestra, dressed in black, with their instruments.

Costel was there too, as he had promised, in a grey suit slightly too tight, a rose in his buttonhole. He stood very straight next to the grandmother, like a bodyguard. Bernard Delorme had come with Marc. Sami’s father wore the new jacket from the Paris trip. Elena had already crossed line number forty-three off her list. She had been crying since noon.

Radu waited at the foot of the steps with Ioana and Chloé, his witnesses. Every thirty seconds he checked that Julien really had the rings. The last time he had proposed to someone, he had left the ring at the hotel. Julien ended up showing him the little box, open, under his nose. “They’re here. They’re not going to fly away. Breathe.”

At five to three, a white car stopped in front of the town hall. Antonio got out first. Then he held out his hand to his daughter. When Lucia appeared, in her white dress with lace sleeves, there was complete silence in the square. Even the pigeons, Odile said later, fell silent. Radu forgot to breathe.

The ceremony lasted twenty minutes. The deputy mayor read the articles of the Civil Code in a warm voice. Lucia said yes in three languages. And when the registrar asked Radu the question, he shouted “YES!” so loudly that the deputy mayor stepped back, and out in the square the orchestra children applauded without knowing why.

Ioana knew why. She squeezed Julien’s hand so hard he nearly shouted too. Odile, in the third row, looked up at the ceiling of the wedding room, decorated with nineteenth-century paintings. “There,” she murmured. “Did you hear it, my dear? He said it for you.”

When the newlyweds came out onto the town hall steps, a shower of rice and rose petals fell on them. The two grandmothers threw the petals side by side, with the same energy, as if they had rehearsed together. And at the bottom of the steps, at a sign from Théo, the sixty children struck up the Spanish tune Lucia had taught them.

Lucia burst into tears. Then she lifted her dress and danced, right there on the town hall steps, in front of astonished passers-by, stamping her feet as she had taught them. A Japanese tourist filmed the whole scene. That very evening, the video had already been seen by thousands of people who would never know who those people were.

At seven, a coach was waiting outside the town hall to take the guests to La Duchère. At the wheel was Costel. He had insisted for three days at the rental agency, in Romanian, in English and with gestures, until they agreed to let him drive. “Twenty years I’ve been driving grandmothers,” he explained to Radu. “Today I’m driving mine.”

The Hélène Morel hall had been transformed. Strings of lights hung from the ceiling, bouquets of white flowers decorated every table, and the little lime tree by the door shone with a thousand tiny bulbs. On a table at the entrance stood the box for the Henri and Hélène scholarship. By the end of the night it would be so full it could no longer be closed.

The ball was to be opened with a waltz. Everyone knew which one. But nobody knew who would conduct the orchestra. When the newlyweds stepped into the middle of the dance floor, Julien stood up, crossed the hall and held out his baton, the one he never used, to Théo. “It’s your orchestra now,” he said. “Begin.”

Théo took the baton in a trembling hand. He looked at the sixty children, who looked back at him with total trust. Then he gave Inès a small sign. Lucien Roux’s clarinet began alone, very softly, the first notes of Henri’s waltz. Radu took Lucia in his arms, and they began to turn.

Radu had never been a good dancer. But that evening he danced as if someone were guiding him. At the third verse, as always, Odile stood up and whistled the melody. This time the grandmother and doña Carmen stood up with her and, not knowing the words, they hummed. Three old ladies, three languages, a single waltz.

Julien, standing at the back of the hall, didn’t watch the bride and groom. He watched Théo. The boy ended up conducting without the baton, because he had put it down on the stand from the first bars. He conducted with his hands, with his eyes, exactly as Julien did. Ioana came over. “Aren’t you sad?” she asked. “No,” Julien answered. “I’m proud. It’s different, but it has the same effect on the eyes.”

After the waltz, Dan gave his speech. He had cut the twelve minutes to four, as Ioana had asked him, and kept only one formal sentence, at the end, for the toast. When he finished with “Allez, on bouffe !”, the hall exploded with laughter. Even Nathalie laughed. Dan, who didn’t understand why it was so funny, bowed like an actor.

Table number four, the one that had worried Radu so much, was the liveliest of the evening. The grandmother, doña Carmen, Odile and Mrs Roux were over three hundred and twenty years old between them, and had not a single language in common. Yet they talked for three hours, with their hands, with their eyes, with drawings on the paper napkins.

Mrs Roux taught them a song from the Villeurbanne brass band, the one Lucien used to play on Sundays. Doña Carmen explained to them, with gestures, how to make a real gazpacho. The grandmother drew the sarmale recipe on three napkins. And Odile told Henri’s story to women who didn’t understand a word of French, and who cried anyway.

Around eleven, don Manuel took his guitar and climbed onto the little stage. He announced that he had composed a song for the bride and groom, and that nobody had heard it yet, except his guitar. It was a slow flamenco, but with, in the middle, a strange, plaintive melody that didn’t come from Andalusia. The grandmother sat up straight in her chair. She had recognised a doina.

Don Manuel had learned the doina by listening to old recordings Lucia had sent him. When he reached that passage, the grandmother stood up and sang with him, in her frail, true voice, the Romanian words nobody else understood. Mihaela, at the back of the hall, took out her țambal hammers and accompanied them.

At midnight, as Romanian tradition demanded, the hora began. Radu took his grandmother’s hand, Lucia took doña Carmen’s, and the circle grew little by little. The Mansouris joined in, then the orchestra children, then Bernard Delorme, who danced badly but with conviction, then Costel, who knew all the steps. Mr Mansouri took out his oud to accompany the țambal.

During the hora, Julien and Ioana slipped away for a few minutes. They went outside in front of the hall, under the little illuminated lime tree. The music reached them muffled through the windows. Julien took Catherine Dumas’s business card out of his pocket. “I’ve decided,” he said. “I’m going to accept. From Lyon. With Théo and Lucia here, two days a week at La Duchère.”

Ioana smiled. “I know,” she answered. “I knew before you did. The evening you came back from Paris, when you emptied your pockets on the table. You put the ministry card next to Sami’s drawing, not next to the list of children.” Julien looked at her, astonished. She shrugged. “I’m an architect. I watch where people put things.”

“But we’re still talking about it at the seaside, on 15 May,” she added. “It’s written in pen. It can’t be erased.” Julien laughed. Then he took her in his arms, under the lime tree, and they danced together to the muffled music of the hora, which wasn’t music for dancing in pairs at all. It didn’t matter in the slightest.

At three in the morning, the grandmother was still dancing. Doña Carmen had fallen asleep in an armchair, her rosary in her hand, smiling. Mrs Roux and Odile were singing the brass band song, out of tune and very loud. Rose-Hélène, who should have been asleep long before, was finally sleeping in Elena’s arms, Henri’s harmonica clutched in her little hand.

In a corner, Marc Delorme was writing in his notebook, by the light of his phone. He was preparing the article for the following week’s neighbourhood paper. He had already found the headline: “A yes heard all the way to Seville”. His uncle, sitting next to him, read over his shoulder. “It’s good,” said Bernard Delorme. “It’s true, and it’s well written. Keep it up.” Marc blushed like a child.

At five, only about thirty people were left. Lucia had taken off her shoes long ago. Radu had lost his tie somewhere between the hora and the flamenco. The two of them went out under the lime tree, barefoot in the cool grass, while the sky began to pale above the La Duchère tower blocks.

That was when Radu took an envelope out of his pocket. “Your honeymoon,” he said. “You asked me a hundred times where we were going.” Lucia opened it. Inside were two plane tickets to Iași, and a photo: an old walnut tree on a hill above a village. “That’s where my father proposed to my mother,” Radu explained. “And Julien to Ioana. I wanted you to see where I come from.”

Lucia looked at the photo for a long time. Then she looked up at him, and he saw she was crying and laughing at the same time. “Do you know what my grandmother told me this morning, when she gave me the dress?” she asked. “She told me that one day I would go to Romania, and I would understand why the piece of ie was sewn on the inside. So that I would wear it close to my heart, without anyone seeing it.”

The sun rose at a quarter past six, red, behind the towers. Its first light fell straight into the big window in the roof of the hall, the one Yanis had drawn, and lit up the inside, where a few guests were still dancing. Radu watched the window shine. He thought of the letter under his pillow, of Hélène’s voice, of the word he had shouted.

“She heard,” he said softly. “Do you think she heard?” Lucia didn’t know who he was talking about, not yet. He would tell her later, under the walnut tree, in Romania. But she laid her head on his shoulder and answered, in French, with her Salamanca accent: “My love, they heard you in Seville.” Behind them, in the hall, Théo gave Inès a sign. The waltz was starting again.

In the evening, at the Hélène Morel hall, Dan finally gives his speech. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear friends, dear family, dear guests from Romania, Spain and France. I am very happy to be with you tonight. My daughter told me that my first speech was too formal. So I started all over again.

When Radu left for Lyon on his Erasmus, he was twenty and he couldn’t boil an egg. His grandmother was afraid he would starve. She sent him sarmale by post for six months. French customs confiscated half of them.

I didn’t think he would stay here. I thought he would come back to Iași after a year. But he met a young woman with a guitar, at midnight, in a student residence. And I think he understood that evening that he wouldn’t be coming home.

Lucia, I am proud that my son chose you. And I am even prouder that you chose him, because, frankly, it wasn’t obvious. He snores, he forgets his keys, and he sings out of tune in the shower. But he has an enormous heart.

If my parents were still alive, if Ion, Radu’s grandfather, were here, if they could all have seen this hall full of music, I think they would have danced until morning. So tonight we will dance for them. And for a lady I never knew, but whose memory everyone here carries a little: Hélène.
I kindly ask you to raise your glasses in honour of the young couple. To Radu and Lucia! For better and for worse. And now, as my son says… come on, let’s eat!
